title: Flowing everywhere
hookLine: the great Tao flows everywhere and claims nothing (Tao Te Ching 34)

lines: THE ONE WHO FIXED IT AT MIDNIGHT.
EVERYWHERE IN THE WORK, NOWHERE ON THE CREDITS.
cards: The last slide of a group presentation is the one with everybody's names on it.
Sometimes there's one person on it who quietly fixed the spreadsheet at midnight, rewrote the clumsy paragraph, and sent the reminder that got everyone there on time.
Their name is on the slide in the same size font as everyone else's. They didn't ask for more.
Chapter thirty-four of the Tao Te Ching describes the Tao a lot like that person: everywhere in the work, and nowhere on the credits.

teach.h: FOUND ON THE LEFT AND ON THE RIGHT.
teach.b: First, the flood. In James Legge's translation the chapter begins: "All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left hand and on the right."
The Chinese word behind all-pervading has the sense of water overflowing, spilling in every direction at once. Not a channel. A flood plain.
Second, no claim. The chapter says all things depend on it to come into being, and it doesn't turn any of them away.
And when the work is done, it doesn't claim the name of having done it. It clothes and feeds everything, and doesn't set itself up as their master.
Third, small and great at once. Because it asks for nothing, the chapter says, it can be called small. And because everything returns to it without even knowing it's there, it can be called great.
The same thing, named both ways. Fourth, the sage.

teach.h: GREAT BY NOT MAKING ITSELF GREAT.
teach.b: The chapter ends by saying the wise person does great things in the same way: by never trying to make himself great. Not hiding. Not pretending to be nothing.
Just not reaching for the name. Credit is everywhere, at work, in families, online: a like, a thank-you, a name in the email. The chapter doesn't call wanting it wicked.
It just describes something enormous that gives without keeping score, and suggests the wise do the same.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-four as a model for giving without seeking credit: doing the work, letting it spread, and not claiming the name for it.

games.q: your project worked, and everyone's asking who was behind it. what would chapter thirty-four's Tao do?
o: step up and take the credit.
finish the work and claim no name for it.
insist it had nothing to do with it.
games.why: when its work is done, the chapter says, it doesn't claim the name of having done it. not denial, not a spotlight: just no claim.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you could do for someone that they may never trace back to you: refill something running low, fix a small thing that's been broken a while, put in a good word when they're not around.
Choose one, and sit with the strange feeling of a gift with no name on it.

wordCard.voice: Flowing everywhere. Chapter thirty-four's great Tao, found on the left hand and the right, feeding everything and claiming none of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: overflowing, flooding; chapter thirty-four's word for the great Tao spreading left and right.

carryVoice: Your line: claim nothing. The work gets done either way. Rest well.
